title: There's a life on every bike
excerpt: The City of Toronto launched a bicycle safety campaign in June 2024 with a simple message: "There's a Life on Every Bike."
content:
The City of Toronto launched a bicycle safety campaign in June 2024 called Driving Safely Near People Cycling. It shares the simple message "There's a Life on Every Bike," intended to remind people driving in Toronto of the safety measures to be taken when sharing roads with people who cycle — to reduce injuries and fatalities.

The campaign was the recipient of a 2025 Applied Arts Award in the Illustration category, and is showcased in the Applied Arts Summer 2025 magazine and their winners' online gallery.

The campaign ran for four weeks, posted on billboards in public spaces and on social media. To view the full campaign, visit toronto.ca/watchforbikes.

title: Brompton Bling (aka Buzz)
excerpt: While commuting I get a lot of questions about my bike. Often, people have not seen a folding bike or seen it in action. Here's how I turned my Brompton into a rolling light show.
content:
While commuting I get a lot of questions about my bike. Often, people have not seen a folding bike or seen it in action. I'm always happy to demonstrate how it folds and allow them to lift it. I like to share stories about riding 65km on the Don Valley Parkway (DVP) and then getting on Via Rail to work in Montreal for a week... all with just my Brompton and what it can carry.

Other times, people are fans of Bromptons or want to know more about the lights. Some of the customizations I've done include:

Customizations

  1. Wheels: White fairy lights from Dollarama ($1.50)... I had to test it for the price and I did it a few hours before a major night time bike event. The fairy lights were only meant to be temporary but I think anyone could make them permanent. The next day, I added what I always intended for the wheels: a 5V, 2.7mm wide, single colour COB LED (480 LED/m, 5W/m), 1m length. I use an optional dimmer controller so I can dim, blink or strobe the lights. The battery packs are small and just barely fit into the Brompton's small wheels. The LEDs are very bright even in daytime and have a continuous Tron-like effect.
  2. Tube: 5V, 3mm wide, addressable RGB COB LED (240 LED/m, 18W/m), about 1.5m. Wrapped around tube and seat post. Viewable on both sides. I use an IoTorero slim WLED controller. Small USB battery and controller tucked into a $3 boomerang bag (AliExpress) designed for the Brompton.
  3. Helmet: Same COB LEDs used on the wheels but in red. I removed the visor to make it a bit more Tron-like. About 1 to 1.5m of LEDs.
  4. Cooler: 5L yellow cooler (AliExpress). Selected because the sides and bottom were flat so the block mount could be added easily. The lid flaps open so I use crystal clear gorilla tape to keep it closed.
  5. Neon sign: Pink "love" neon sign from Canadian Tire, powered by 3x AA. I have another that is a yellow "hello". Hard not to buy more — banana, palm tree, cherries... I just tape them to whatever I have on the block mount.
  6. High visibility vest: Probably what I've spent the most time experimenting with. Started with electroluminescent (EL) wire wrapped around my torso, then moved to 5m of single colour COB LEDs stitched to a vest. Now the COB LEDs are 4m in length and follow the reflective fabric so well that people don't usually notice until it's on.
  7. Future ideas: RGB on the tires, another helmet with RGB, and RGB on the Brompton stem. I'm careful about additions to the Brompton as I don't want to interfere with the fold — which is why I started with wearables.

Parts used

  • 5V addressable RGB COB LEDs
  • 5V single-colour COB LEDs
  • LED dimmer (for single-colour LEDs)
  • WLED controller (for RGB LEDs)
  • 21700 5000mAh Li-ion battery
  • Powerbank holder/charger

title: Position yourself for safety
excerpt: I commute daily through downtown rush hour traffic and frequently see situations cyclists and drivers may not fully understand. The short answer: know the rules and ride predictably.
content:
In addition to my regular fun rides, I commute daily. Rain or shine. Summer and winter. My commutes are downtown in rush hour traffic and I frequently see situations some cyclists and drivers may not fully understand (I admit I had to do some research myself).

Who has the right of way? What is the safe thing to do? The short answer is, know the rules and ride predictably.

In my opinion, it's more important to be safe than it is to be "right".

The unfortunate reality is, cyclists are more vulnerable on the roads compared to cars, trucks and other motorized vehicles. In the event of any distractions, errors or collisions, it's the cyclist that suffers the most injuries (or is even killed). Cyclists can reduce these risks by riding predictably and positioning themselves for safety.

Positioning yourself for safety starts with understanding the rules and what is expected of cyclists and drivers.

Vehicles turning right

Many cyclists are aware of the "right hook", when a driver turns right into the path of a cyclist. Here are two examples that many cyclists and drivers may not understand — something I see every day that few seem to get right.

Solid line

When there is a solid line leading to the intersection, the cyclist has the right of way. Vehicles must not enter the bicycle lane until they can safely turn into the opposing lane, yielding to cyclists and pedestrians.

Dashed line

When there is a dashed line leading to the intersection, this allows drivers to fully enter the bike lane when it is safe and clear of cyclists. Cyclists must then pass the turning vehicle on the left or wait behind the vehicle until the lane is clear.

Cyclists should not attempt to squeeze past the vehicle on the right. This is unsafe for the cyclist, causes confusion and slows traffic for cyclists and other vehicles.

What should a cyclist do?

  1. Follow the rules and ride predictably! If another vehicle isn't yielding the right of way or is driving unsafely — let them go. Don't place yourself between them and where they want to go. Be prepared to stop and wait behind others or pass them on the left if it is safe.
  2. Visit the Toronto Police Service website to file a police report and submit a "driving complaint" (Note: a driving complaint also applies to vehicles stopped in cycle tracks, bike lanes or no stopping zones).

title: Legend of Roman Freely
excerpt: Last night I had the honor of riding with the spirit of Roman Freely. Not everyone is aware of who Roman is so I'd like to share the story…
content:
Last night I had the honor of riding with the spirit of Roman Freely. Not everyone is aware of who Roman is so I'd like to share the story…

Every Halloween night, when the fog rolls down from Casa Loma and the streetlights flicker on Queen West, cyclists whisper about a rider who never unclipped. His name was Roman Freely.

Roman founded The Neon Riders back in the 80s with Jack Layton. They believed LED lights could open portals to parallel bike lanes… smoother, Ford-free dimensions known only as The Eternal Pathway. He was known for his disco-ball rear reflector, and habit of shouting "Stay visible or stay ghostly!" at anyone riding without lights.

But one fateful Halloween night, during the legendary Midnight Spoke Parade of 1995, Roman took a wrong turn down an unmarked lane near the Don Valley… and never returned.

Some say he merged with the Toronto Bike Share system and now haunts any rider who forgets to dock their bike on time.

Every October 31st, people claim to see his spectral form — a blur of neon orange and flickering LEDs — cruising along Bloor, blasting '80s synthwave from nowhere, leaving a faint smell of pumpkin spice chain lube in his wake.

If you hear the squeak of a ghostly brake and feel your bike lights flicker, don't be afraid. Just whisper:

Ride on, Roman Freely... ride on.

title: Why Cycling Changed My Life
excerpt: In spring 2024 I was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. What happened next surprised me.
content:
In spring 2024, I received a diagnosis I wasn't expecting — fatty liver disease. My doctor was direct about what needed to change: my diet, my activity level, and my relationship with movement. I'd heard it before, but this time it landed differently.

Finding the bike

That summer I started cycling. Nothing dramatic at first — short rides around the neighbourhood, getting comfortable on the saddle. But something clicked. It didn't feel like exercise. It felt like going somewhere.

By fall I had lost 40 pounds. More importantly, I had found a way to move through the world that felt sustainable, even joyful. Cycling became my commute, not just my workout.

What the road taught me

Cycling as a daily commuter in a car-first city teaches you things quickly. You learn which roads have safe shoulders, which intersections are designed without you in mind, and how invisible you can feel to drivers who are simply not looking for you.

It also taught me why cycling matters — not just for health, but for how we design cities, how we share space, and how we treat each other on the road. That's what this site is about.
